bibl.title: Sarcopenia: European consensus on definition and diagnosis: Report of the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: A WORKING GROUP DEFINING A CONDITION THAT HAD BEEN NAMED FOR TWENTY-ONE YEARS - four European societies convened to give sarcopenia a clinical definition, diagnostic criteria and cut-off points, because it had none
span.quote: While age-related sarcopenia is common and has huge personal and financial costs, sarcopenia still has no broadly accepted clinical definition, consensus diagnostic criteria, International Classification of Diseases 9th Revision (ICD-9) codes or treatment guidelines.

span.label: what sarcopenia is, what parameters define it, which variables measure those parameters, at what cut-off points, and how it relates to cachexia, frailty and sarcopenic obesity
span.quote: Sarcopenia is a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with a risk of adverse outcomes such as physical disability, poor quality of life and death [ 17, 18 ]. The EWGSOP recommends using the presence of both low muscle mass and low muscle function (strength or performance) for the diagnosis of sarcopenia.

span.label: the EWGSOP definition - low muscle mass PLUS low muscle function - with three conceptual stages (presarcopenia, sarcopenia, severe sarcopenia), a primary/secondary category split, a table of cut-off points from the literature, and a gait-speed case-finding algorithm
span.quote: Sarcopenia is a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with a risk of adverse outcomes such as physical disability, poor quality of life and death [ 17, 18 ]. The EWGSOP recommends using the presence of both low muscle mass and low muscle function (strength or performance) for the diagnosis of sarcopenia.

span.label: method
span.quote: Sarcopenia is a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with a risk of adverse outcomes such as physical disability, poor quality of life and death [ 17, 18 ]. The EWGSOP recommends using the presence of both low muscle mass and low muscle function (strength or performance) for the diagnosis of sarcopenia.

span.label: a term in wide use whose prevalence estimate depends on which definition of it the estimator chose
span.quote: Depending on the literature definition used for sarcopenia, the prevalence in 60–70-year-olds is reported as 5–13%, while the prevalence ranges from 11 to 50% in people >80 years [ 71 ].

span.label: consensus working group: four societies nominated representatives, three meetings in 2009 plus extensive email, literature reviews guided by four questions, then circulation to the four boards for input, revision and final endorsement
span.term: consensus working group: four societies nominated representatives, three meetings in 2009 plus extensive email, literature reviews guided by four questions, then circulation to the four boards for input, revision and final endorsement
span.quote: While age-related sarcopenia is common and has huge personal and financial costs, sarcopenia still has no broadly accepted clinical definition, consensus diagnostic criteria, International Classification of Diseases 9th Revision (ICD-9) codes or treatment guidelines.

span.label: A TERM COINED IN 1989 THAT STILL HAD NO AGREED DEFINITION IN 2010: `In 1989, IRWIN ROSENBERG PROPOSED THE TERM `SARCOPENIA` (GREEK `SARX` OR FLESH + `PENIA` OR LOSS) to describe this age-related decrease of muscle mass. Sarcopenia has since been defined as the loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength that occurs with advancing age. However, A WIDELY ACCEPTED DEFINITION OF SARCOPENIA SUITABLE FOR USE IN RESEARCH AND CLINICAL PRACTICE IS STILL LACKING.` The coinage is dated, attributed and given its etymology, and the gap it left is stated in the next sentence
span.quote: In 1989, Irwin Rosenberg proposed the term ‘sarcopenia’ (Greek ‘sarx’ or flesh + ‘penia’ or loss) to describe this age-related decrease of muscle mass [ 1, 2 ]. Sarcopenia has since been defined as the loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength that occurs with advancing age [ 3 ]. However, a widely accepted definition of sarcopenia suitable for use in research and clinical practice is still lacking.

span.label: AND THE ABSENCE IS ENUMERATED, INCLUDING THE ADMINISTRATIVE ONE: `sarcopenia still has NO BROADLY ACCEPTED CLINICAL DEFINITION, CONSENSUS DIAGNOSTIC CRITERIA, INTERNATIONAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES 9TH REVISION (ICD-9) CODES OR TREATMENT GUIDELINES.` A missing ICD code is a missing SLOT IN A CONTROLLED VOCABULARY, listed beside the missing definition as the same kind of lack - the clearest statement in this corpus that a definition and its administrative code are one problem
span.quote: While age-related sarcopenia is common and has huge personal and financial costs, sarcopenia still has no broadly accepted clinical definition, consensus diagnostic criteria, International Classification of Diseases 9th Revision (ICD-9) codes or treatment guidelines.

span.label: AND A BETTER TERM WAS REJECTED BECAUSE THE WORSE ONE IS ALREADY KNOWN: `Some have argued that THE TERM DYNAPENIA IS BETTER SUITED to describe age-associated loss of muscle strength and function. However, SARCOPENIA IS ALREADY A WIDELY RECOGNISED TERM, SO REPLACING IT MIGHT LEAD TO FURTHER CONFUSION.` **THE EXACT MIRROR OF haas2018**: Banff DELETED the word `acute` because it confused clinicians; EWGSOP KEPT `sarcopenia`, against a term it concedes is better suited, because replacing it would confuse. Two consensus bodies, opposite decisions, the same reason - and neither decision is about the biology
span.quote: Some have argued that the term dynapenia is better suited to describe age-associated loss of muscle strength and function [ 20 ]. However, sarcopenia is already a widely recognised term, so replacing it might lead to further confusion.

span.label: AND THE PREVALENCE RANGE IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE DEFINITION IN ONE SENTENCE: `DEPENDING ON THE LITERATURE DEFINITION USED FOR SARCOPENIA, the prevalence in 60-70-year-olds is reported as 5-13%, while the prevalence ranges from 11 TO 50% in people >80 years.` bellomo2004 and hoste2006 each gave a range and left the reader to infer the cause; this paper names it
span.quote: Depending on the literature definition used for sarcopenia, the prevalence in 60–70-year-olds is reported as 5–13%, while the prevalence ranges from 11 to 50% in people >80 years [ 71 ].

span.label: AND A THRESHOLD SET BY WHAT DATA EXISTED, CALLED ARBITRARY BY THE PAPER ITSELF: `BECAUSE POPULATION NORMS FOR YOUNG ADULT BLACKS AND WHITES ARE NOT CURRENTLY AVAILABLE, the gender-specific 20TH PERCENTILE WAS ARBITRARILY CHOSEN as the cut-off point for each method.` The class boundary is where the reference data ran out, and the sentence says which population's absence set it
span.quote: Because population norms for young adult blacks and whites are not currently available, the gender-specific 20th percentile was arbitrarily chosen as the cut-off point for each method.

span.label: AND THE CONVENTION BEHIND EVERY OTHER CUT-OFF IS STATED AS A CHOICE: `EWGSOP recommends use of NORMATIVE (HEALTHY YOUNG ADULT) RATHER THAN OTHER PREDICTIVE REFERENCE POPULATIONS, with cut-off points at TWO STANDARD DEVIATIONS BELOW THE MEAN reference value. MORE RESEARCH IS URGENTLY NEEDED IN ORDER TO OBTAIN GOOD REFERENCE VALUES FOR POPULATIONS AROUND THE WORLD.` Two decisions - which population is the reference, and how many SDs below it - and the paper concedes the first is under-supplied
span.quote: Cut-off points depend upon the measurement technique chosen and on the availability of reference studies. EWGSOP recommends use of normative (healthy young adult) rather than other predictive reference populations, with cut-off points at two standard deviations below the mean reference value. More research is urgently needed in order to obtain good reference values for populations around the world.

span.label: AND THE INTENSION IS DECLARED TOO NARROW, WITH THE REASON: `muscle strength DOES NOT DEPEND SOLELY ON MUSCLE MASS, and the relationship between strength and mass IS NOT LINEAR. Thus, DEFINING SARCOPENIA ONLY IN TERMS OF MUSCLE MASS IS TOO NARROW and may be of limited clinical value.` The two-criterion rule is derived from a non-linearity rather than asserted
span.quote: The rationale for use of two criteria is: muscle strength does not depend solely on muscle mass, and the relationship between strength and mass is not linear [ 18, 19 ]. Thus, defining sarcopenia only in terms of muscle mass is too narrow and may be of limited clinical value.

span.label: and the category is adopted BECAUSE the causes are unknown, not despite it: `We suggest it may be likewise helpful to RECOGNISE SARCOPENIA AS A GERIATRIC SYNDROME BECAUSE THIS VIEW PROMOTES ITS IDENTIFICATION AND TREATMENT EVEN WHEN THE EXACT CAUSES REMAIN UNKNOWN.` A class chosen for what it lets clinicians do, with the aetiological ignorance stated as part of the justification
span.quote: We suggest it may be likewise helpful to recognise sarcopenia as a geriatric syndrome because this view promotes its identification and treatment even when the exact causes remain unknown [ 5, 6 ].

span.label: THE NEIGHBOURING CONSTRUCTS OVERLAP ASYMMETRICALLY AND ONE IS PART OF THE OTHER'S DEFINITION: `most cachectic individuals are also sarcopenic, BUT MOST SARCOPENIC INDIVIDUALS ARE NOT CONSIDERED CACHECTIC. SARCOPENIA IS ONE OF THE ELEMENTS OF THE PROPOSED DEFINITION FOR CACHEXIA.` A concept that is a COMPONENT OF ANOTHER CONCEPT'S DEFINITION while also being distinguished from it - the corpus has no edge type for `is part of the definition of`, only for parts of things
span.quote: Cachexia is frequently associated with inflammation, insulin resistance, anorexia and increased breakdown of muscle proteins [ 23, 24 ]. Thus, most cachectic individuals are also sarcopenic, but most sarcopenic individuals are not considered cachectic. Sarcopenia is one of the elements of the proposed definition for cachexia [ 22 ].

span.label: AND FRAILTY OVERLAPS IT WHILE EXTENDING BEYOND IT: `FRAILTY AND SARCOPENIA OVERLAP; most frail older people exhibit sarcopenia, and some older people with sarcopenia are also frail. The general concept of frailty, however, GOES BEYOND PHYSICAL FACTORS TO ENCOMPASS PSYCHOLOGICAL AND SOCIAL DIMENSIONS as well.` Overlap without containment in either direction, said in one sentence
span.quote: Frailty and sarcopenia overlap; most frail older people exhibit sarcopenia, and some older people with sarcopenia are also frail. The general concept of frailty, however, goes beyond physical factors to encompass psychological and social dimensions as well, including cognitive status, social support and other environmental factors [ 26 ].

span.label: and there is no standard outcome to test a treatment against: `only a handful of clinical trials are under way to test potential sarcopenia treatments. THE ABSENCE OF STANDARDISED PRIMARY OUTCOMES IS A MAJOR CHALLENGE FOR THE DESIGN OF SUCH STUDIES.` The definition is proposed so that trials become possible, and the paper says in the same paragraph that the outcomes for those trials do not exist either
span.quote: While reduced mobility and functionality are increasingly prevalent in older people, only a handful of clinical trials are under way to test potential sarcopenia treatments. The absence of standardised primary outcomes is a major challenge for the design of such studies. For intervention trials, EWGSOP presently recommends three primary outcome variables—muscle mass, muscle strength and physical performance

span.label: and the stages are labelled CONCEPTUAL, with presarcopenia reachable only by an instrument most clinics do not have: `THIS STAGE CAN ONLY BE IDENTIFIED BY TECHNIQUES THAT MEASURE MUSCLE MASS ACCURATELY AND IN REFERENCE TO STANDARD POPULATIONS` - so the first stage of the classification is, in practice, unobservable wherever the reference populations are the ones the paper says are missing
span.quote: The ‘presarcopenia’ stage is characterised by low muscle mass without impact on muscle strength or physical performance. This stage can only be identified by techniques that measure muscle mass accurately and in reference to standard populations. The ‘sarcopenia’ stage is characterised by low muscle mass, plus low muscle strength or low physical performance. ‘Severe sarcopenia’ is the stage identified when all three criteria of the definition are met (low muscle mass, low muscle strength and low physical performance).

span.label: requiring BOTH low muscle mass and low muscle function for the diagnosis, rather than mass alone
span.note: eliminates: a definition that the paper argues is too narrow, on the grounds that `muscle strength does not depend solely on muscle mass, and the relationship between strength and mass is not linear` · outcome: held
span.quote: The rationale for use of two criteria is: muscle strength does not depend solely on muscle mass, and the relationship between strength and mass is not linear [ 18, 19 ]. Thus, defining sarcopenia only in terms of muscle mass is too narrow and may be of limited clinical value.

span.label: normative (healthy young adult) reference populations rather than predictive ones, with cut-offs two standard deviations below the mean
span.note: eliminates: cut-off points that drift with whichever study population happens to be at hand · outcome: partial
span.quote: Cut-off points depend upon the measurement technique chosen and on the availability of reference studies. EWGSOP recommends use of normative (healthy young adult) rather than other predictive reference populations, with cut-off points at two standard deviations below the mean reference value. More research is urgently needed in order to obtain good reference values for populations around the world.

span.label: the primary/secondary split by whether a cause other than ageing is evident
span.note: eliminates: treating disease-, activity- and nutrition-related muscle loss as age-related sarcopenia · outcome: partial
span.quote: Thus, the categories of primary sarcopenia and secondary sarcopenia may be useful in clinical practice. Sarcopenia can be considered ‘primary’ (or age-related) when no other cause is evident but ageing itself, while sarcopenia can be considered ‘secondary’ when one or more other causes are evident ( Table 2 ). In many older people, the aetiology of sarcopenia is multi-factorial so that it may not be possible to characterise each individual as having a primary or secondary condition.

span.label: sarcopenia
span.quote: Sarcopenia is a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with a risk of adverse outcomes such as physical disability, poor quality of life and death [ 17, 18 ]. The EWGSOP recommends using the presence of both low muscle mass and low muscle function (strength or performance) for the diagnosis of sarcopenia.

span.label: `sarcopenia` (Rosenberg 1989) - the COINAGE: Greek `sarx` (flesh) + `penia` (loss), for the age-related decrease of muscle MASS alone
span.quote: In 1989, Irwin Rosenberg proposed the term ‘sarcopenia’ (Greek ‘sarx’ or flesh + ‘penia’ or loss) to describe this age-related decrease of muscle mass [ 1, 2 ]. Sarcopenia has since been defined as the loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength that occurs with advancing age [ 3 ]. However, a widely accepted definition of sarcopenia suitable for use in research and clinical practice is still lacking.

span.label: `sarcopenia` (EWGSOP 2010) - MASS PLUS FUNCTION: `a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass AND STRENGTH`, diagnosed as low muscle mass PLUS low muscle strength or low physical performance. The 1989 sense is declared `TOO NARROW`
span.quote: Sarcopenia is a syndrome characterised by progressive and generalised loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength with a risk of adverse outcomes such as physical disability, poor quality of life and death [ 17, 18 ]. The EWGSOP recommends using the presence of both low muscle mass and low muscle function (strength or performance) for the diagnosis of sarcopenia.

span.label: `dynapenia` - the term EWGSOP concedes is `BETTER SUITED to describe age-associated loss of muscle strength and function`, and declines to adopt because `sarcopenia is already a widely recognised term`

span.label: `primary` vs `secondary sarcopenia` - the same condition split by whether a cause OTHER THAN AGEING is evident; the paper adds that in many older people the aetiology is multi-factorial so neither label applies

Sarcopenia can be considered ‘primary’ (or age-related) when no other cause is evident but ageing itself, while sarcopenia can be considered ‘secondary’ when one or more other causes are evident ( Table 2 ). In many older people, the aetiology of sarcopenia is multi-factorial so that it may not be possible to characterise each individual as having a primary or secondary condition.

span.label: `presarcopenia` / `sarcopenia` / `severe sarcopenia` - three CONCEPTUAL stages by how many of the three criteria are met
span.quote: The ‘presarcopenia’ stage is characterised by low muscle mass without impact on muscle strength or physical performance. This stage can only be identified by techniques that measure muscle mass accurately and in reference to standard populations. The ‘sarcopenia’ stage is characterised by low muscle mass, plus low muscle strength or low physical performance. ‘Severe sarcopenia’ is the stage identified when all three criteria of the definition are met (low muscle mass, low muscle strength and low physical performance).

span.label: extends → Rosenberg's 1989 coinage of `sarcopenia` for the age-related decrease of muscle mass - this paper keeps the name and widens the intension to require function

However, a widely accepted definition of sarcopenia suitable for use in research and clinical practice is still lacking.

Sarcopenia is ONE OF THE ELEMENTS OF THE PROPOSED DEFINITION FOR CACHEXIA.` Distinct, asymmetrically overlapping, and one is a component of the other's DEFINITION - which the schema cannot say, so it is in the note

span.quote: Cut-off points depend upon the measurement technique chosen and on the availability of reference studies. EWGSOP recommends use of normative (healthy young adult) rather than other predictive reference populations, with cut-off points at two standard deviations below the mean reference value. More research is urgently needed in order to obtain good reference values for populations around the world.

span.label: `BECAUSE POPULATION NORMS FOR YOUNG ADULT BLACKS AND WHITES ARE NOT CURRENTLY AVAILABLE`
span.term: cut-off used when no normative data existed
span.quote: Because population norms for young adult blacks and whites are not currently available, the gender-specific 20th percentile was arbitrarily chosen as the cut-off point for each method.

span.label: the instrument of the class boundary: two SDs below a normative mean is what makes a measurement `low`, so the reference population chooses the diagnosis

span.quote: The rationale for use of two criteria is: muscle strength does not depend solely on muscle mass, and the relationship between strength and mass is not linear [ 18, 19 ]. Thus, defining sarcopenia only in terms of muscle mass is too narrow and may be of limited clinical value.
